body.p: On January 7, 2019, the Office has published the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance (hereinafter, the "Revised Guidelines") which "supersedes MPEP 2106/04(11) ... along with any other portion of the MPEP that conflicts with this guidance"

(Emphasis added). Under the Revised Guidelines, the Alice/Mayo Step 2A analysis is a two- prong inquiry. "In Prong One, examiners evaluate whether the claim recites a judicial exception," and if the claim is found to recite a judicial exception, in Prong Two, "examiners evaluate whether the claim recites additional elements that integrate the exception into a practical application of that exception." If the claim is found to integrate the recited exception into a practical application of that exception, the claim is patent eligible.

Under the Revised Guidelines, Prong One of Revised Step 2A has been changed. "To determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea in Prong One, examiners are now to: (a) Identify the specific limitation(s) in the claim under examination (individually or in combination) that the examiner believes recites an abstract idea; and (b) determine whether the identified limitation(s) falls within the subject matter groupings of abstract ideas enumerated in Section I of
the 2019 Revised Patent Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance." The groupings of abstract ideas in the Revised Guidelines are:
(a) Mathematical concepts-mathematical relationships, mathematical
formulas or equations, mathematical calculations;

(b) Certain methods of organizing human activity-fundamental economic principles or practices (including hedging, insurance, mitigating risk); commercial or legal interactions (including agreements in the form of contracts; legal obligations; advertising, marketing or sales activities or behaviors; business relations); managing personal behavior or relationships or interactions between people (including social activities,
teaching, and following rules or instructions); and
(c) Mental processes-concepts performed in the human mind (including
an observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion).

The Office Action contends that the claimed method falls within the "Mental processes" grouping of abstract ideas. However, the features of "wherein acquiring the detection region corresponding to the first operation comprises:

body.p: wherein the first terminal device comprises a display screen and a processor, the display screen is configured for presenting the graphical user interface, and the processor is configured for running a game, generating the graphical user interface, and controlling display of the graphical user interface on the display screen" cannot be practically applied in the human mind.

According to the Revised Guidelines, "claims that do not recite matter that falls within these enumerated groupings of abstract ideas should not be treated as reciting abstract ideas" (emphasis added). Applicant respectfully submits that none of the claimed subject matter falls into any of the three subject matter groupings of abstract ideas as set forth in the Revised Guidelines. For this reason alone, the claims of the present application are not directed to an abstract idea and constitute patent eligible subject matter.

The USPTO's Revised Guidelines does provide one narrow exception to the above- discussed rule, describing "the rare circumstance in which a USPTO employee believes a claim limitation that does not fall within the enumerated groupings of abstract ideas should nonetheless be treated as reciting an abstract idea" (emphasis added). In the event a claim that does not fall within one of the three groupings of abstract ideas is treated as being patent ineligible after analysis at Prong Two of Revised Step 2A (discussed below), the rejection "must be approved by the Technology Center Director (which approval will be indicated in the file record of the application), and [the examiner] must provide a justification for why such claim limitation is being treated as reciting an abstract idea."

Assuming, arguendo, that the Office nonetheless considers the claimed subject matter recites an abstract idea falling within one of the three above-discussed groupings of abstract ideas, Applicant respectfully submits that any such alleged abstract idea "is integrated into a practical application of that exception," rendering it patent eligible. As set forth in the USPTO's Revised Guidelines:

"A claim that integrates a judicial exception into a practical application will apply, rely on, or use the judicial exception in a manner that imposes a meaningful limit on the judicial exception, such that the claim is more than a drafting effort designed to monopolize the judicial exception. When the exception is so integrated, then the claim is not directed to a judicial
exception (Step 2A: NO) and is eligible."

"Examiners should note, however, that revised Step 2A specifically excludes consideration of whether the additional elements represent well- understood, routine, conventional activity. Instead, analysis of well- understood, routine, conventional activity is done in Step 2B.
Accordingly, in revised Step 2A examiners should ensure that they give weight to all additional elements, whether or not they are conventional,
when evaluating whether a judicial exception has been integrated into a
practical application."

"Only when a claim recites a judicial exception and fails to integrate the exception into a practical application, is the claim 'directed to' a judicial exception, thereby triggering the need for further analysis pursuant to the
second step of the Alice/Mayo test (USPTO Step 2B)."

Applicants respectfully submit that the claims integrate a practical application, thus are not directed to an abstract idea. Specifically, claim 1 now recites elements such as "wherein the detection region is displayed in a preset state, and the preset state is a state of a light bar, highlighting, or a floating window;

body.p: wherein the first terminal device comprises a display screen and a processor, the display screen is configured for presenting the graphical user interface, and the processor is configured for running a game, generating the graphical user interface, and controlling display of the graphical user interface on the display screen". As described in the specification, a problem being solved is as the size of the screen of the terminal device becomes larger and larger, it is impossible to effectively realize the selection of all game interactive objects in the case of one- handed operation only by adjusting the positions of the game interactive objects. That is, the amended claim 1 is applied to a specific application. Thus, even when the claims are considered under Prong Two of Revised Step 2A, Applicant respectfully submits that the claims are patent eligible under this test as well.

Accordingly, in view of the Revised Guidelines, Applicant respectfully requests that the rejection of claims 1-13 and 15-21 under 35 U.S.C. § 101 be withdrawn because these claims are directed to overcome the problem that the selection of all game entry regions cannot be effectively achieved in the case of one-handed operation, which does not fall into any of subject matter groupings of abstract ideas and is integrated into a practical application.

"Step 2B [of the Alice test] asks: Does the claim recite additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception? Examiners should answer this question by first identifying whether there are any additional elements (features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception(s), and then evaluating those additional elements individually and in combination to determine whether they contribute an inventive concept." MPEP § 2106.05 n.
As amended, the pending claims recite features of "wherein the detection region is displayed in a preset state, and the preset state is a state of a light bar, highlighting, or a floating window;

body.p: wherein the first terminal device comprises a display screen and a processor, the display screen is configured for presenting the graphical user interface, and the processor is configured for running a game, generating the graphical user interface, and controlling display of the graphical user interface on the display screen". Applicants respectfully submit that these features represent an inventive concept. These operations are not well-understood, routine, or conventional, e.g., are significantly more than any law of nature, natural phenomenon, or an abstract idea. Through amended claim 1, by means of acquiring a detection region corresponding to a first operation and by means of acquiring at least one game interaction object which overlaps the detection region, a selection control corresponding to each game interaction object can be provided in a display region, and the selection of a game interaction object is realized on the basis of the selection control, such that the selection of each game interaction object can be realized quickly and conveniently when a single-handed operation is implemented; by displaying the detection region in a preset state, the user can quickly and clearly determine the location of the detection region, so as to make timely adjustment. The effect is significant.
Applicants respectfully request that the rejections be withdrawn.
Claims 1-4, 9-11, 13, 15-16, 18 and 21 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) as being anticipated by Huang et al Ganesan et al, (US 2011 /0179449).

Without acquiescing on the merits of the rejections, by way of this Amendment and Reply, Applicant has amended independent claim 1, and the rejections are believed moot. To the extent that the Office might still apply the rejections to the claim as amended, the rejections are respectfully traversed.

Amended independent claims 13 and 15, although different in scope, each recite similar elements.

According to Huang, it merely discloses a method for selecting a virtual object in a game, including: in response to a first touch operation acting on a graphical user interface, determining a touch point corresponding to the first touch operation on the graphical user interface; determining a plurality of virtual objects meeting preset conditions with the positions of the touch points; generating an object selection control based on the virtual objects, wherein the object selection control comprises a plurality of object identifiers; in response to a second touch operation acting on the object selection control, determining at least one object identifier according to the second touch operation, and selecting the virtual object corresponding to the object identifier.

It can be seen that Huang merely discloses determining the touch point and finding the virtual object that meets the preset conditions with the position of the touch point. Huang does not disclose the technical feature of "acquiring a detection region corresponding to a first operation in response to the first operation acting on the graphical user interface, wherein the detection region is displayed in a preset state, and the preset state is a state of a light bar, highlighting, or a floating window,

acquiring the detection region in accordance with a touch point of the first operation, wherein the detection region is a region with a preset length and a preset width in a preset direction of the first operation by serving the touch point as a starting point" as recited in amended claim 1.

In addition, in the claimed embodiment, each selection control in a display region corresponds to one game interactive object, such that the user can select the required game interaction object with one hand. However, in Huang, the object selection control contains a plurality of object identifiers. In response to the second touch operation on the object selection control, at least one object identifier is determined according to the operation, and the corresponding virtual object is selected. Therefore, Huang does not disclose the feature of
"wherein each selection control corresponds to one game interactive object" as recited in amended claim 1.

Therefore, Huang fails to disclose, teach or suggest at least the features of "acquiring a detection region corresponding to a first operation in response to the first operation acting on the graphical user interface, wherein the detection region is displayed in a preset state, and the preset state is a state of a light bar, highlighting, or a floating window;
wherein each selection control corresponds to one game interactive object; and

acquiring the detection region in accordance with a touch point of the first operation, wherein the detection region is a region with a preset length and a preset width in a preset direction of the first operation by serving the touch point as a starting point" as recited in in amended claim 1, or similar features of amended independent claims 13 and 15.

In view of the above, amended independent claims 1, 13 and 15 are patentable over the reference for at least the reasons set forth above. Their respectively-associated dependent claims are also patentable for at least the same reasons.
Accordingly, withdrawal of the rejections is respectfully requested.
